title: Study of Compounds: Ammonia
tagline: Examine the preparation, properties, reactions and uses of ammonia.

overview.intro: Ammonia (NH3) is a colourless, pungent alkaline gas with high solubility in water, forming ammonium hydroxide. It plays an important role in laboratory chemistry and industry, especially in fertilizers and manufacture of chemicals. This chapter covers laboratory preparation from ammonium salts, collection and drying, physical and chemical properties, tests, and key reactions including its basic nature, reducing behaviour in selected contexts, and reactions with acids and metal salt solutions.

learningOutcomes: Describe laboratory preparation, drying and collection of ammonia gas.

blocks.text: Ammonia is prepared in the laboratory by heating an ammonium salt, such as ammonium chloride, with an alkali like calcium hydroxide (slaked lime). The reaction produces ammonia gas, water and a calcium salt: 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 → CaCl2 + 2H2O + 2NH3↑. The mixture is heated gently in a round-bottom flask.

Ammonia is lighter than air and extremely soluble in water, so it is collected by downward displacement of air (upward delivery) and cannot be collected over water. It is dried using quicklime (CaO), which does not react with basic ammonia. Acidic drying agents such as concentrated sulphuric acid and anhydrous calcium chloride (which forms complexes) are unsuitable.

items: Use an alkali with an ammonium salt to liberate ammonia.
Collect by upward delivery because ammonia is lighter than air.
Dry with quicklime; avoid acidic drying agents.
Do not heat ammonium nitrate or use unsuitable reactants in this preparation.

blocks.text: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a characteristic pungent smell. It is lighter than air and highly soluble in water, forming an alkaline solution called ammonium hydroxide (aqueous ammonia). This solution contains NH4+ and OH− ions and turns red litmus blue.

The fountain experiment demonstrates ammonia’s high solubility. A flask filled with dry ammonia is connected to water containing red litmus. When water enters, ammonia dissolves rapidly, reducing pressure and drawing water up as a fountain that turns blue, indicating the alkaline nature of the solution formed.

items.note: Dissolution in water produces an alkaline solution.

items.text: Fountain experiment: red litmus solution turns blue inside the flask.
items.note: Shows both high solubility and basic character.

learn.title: Chemical Properties: Basic Nature and Reactions

blocks.text: Ammonia is a basic gas. It reacts with acids to form ammonium salts, for example with hydrogen chloride to form dense white fumes of ammonium chloride. Aqueous ammonia neutralises acids to form ammonium salts and water, behaving as a weak alkali.

Ammonia solution reacts with solutions of certain metal salts to precipitate insoluble metal hydroxides. In some cases, such as with copper(II) and zinc salts, the precipitate dissolves in excess ammonia solution due to formation of soluble complex ions. These reactions are useful in qualitative analysis.

blocks.caption: Reactions of ammonia solution with selected metal ions

blocks.text: Ammonia can act as a reducing agent in certain reactions because it contains nitrogen in a low oxidation state and can be oxidised. For example, ammonia reduces heated copper(II) oxide to copper while being oxidised to nitrogen and water: 2NH3 + 3CuO → 3Cu + 3H2O + N2. Such reactions illustrate the chemical reactivity of ammonia beyond its basic nature.

Ammonia burns in oxygen with a greenish-yellow flame under suitable conditions, forming nitrogen and water, and can be catalytically oxidised in industrial processes. At the ICSE level, emphasis is placed on recognising reducing behaviour in specified reactions and writing balanced equations.

items.meaning: A solution of ammonia in water, often represented as ammonium hydroxide.
A salt containing the NH4+ ion, formed when ammonia reacts with acids.
A substance that causes reduction of another substance and is itself oxidised.

blocks.text: Ammonia can be identified by its pungent smell (with caution), by turning moist red litmus paper blue, and by forming dense white fumes with hydrogen chloride gas. These tests distinguish it from neutral or acidic gases. In solution, its alkaline reactions provide further confirmation.

Ammonia is widely used in the manufacture of fertilizers (such as ammonium salts and urea), nitric acid, explosives and cleaning agents. Due to its irritating nature, it should be handled in well-ventilated areas and inhalation should be avoided.

items: Moist red litmus turns blue in presence of ammonia.
Dense white fumes with HCl indicate formation of ammonium chloride.
Use upward delivery and quicklime drying in preparation.
Handle with care to avoid irritation to eyes and respiratory tract.

keyPoints: Ammonia is prepared by heating an ammonium salt with an alkali such as calcium hydroxide.
It is lighter than air and highly soluble in water, so collected by upward delivery and not over water.
Quicklime is used to dry ammonia; acidic drying agents are unsuitable.
Aqueous ammonia is alkaline and turns moist red litmus blue.
Ammonia reacts with acids to form ammonium salts, including white fumes with HCl.
With some metal salt solutions, ammonia forms hydroxide precipitates; Cu2+ and Zn2+ dissolve in excess.
Ammonia can act as a reducing agent, e.g. reducing heated copper(II) oxide.
Balanced equations should show correct reactants, products and conditions.
Fountain experiment demonstrates high solubility and basic nature.
Safety and correct handling are important due to pungent, irritating fumes.

questions.prompt: Ammonia gas is collected by:
questions.answer: upward delivery
questions.explanation: Ammonia is lighter than air and highly soluble in water, so it is collected by upward delivery.
questions.commonMistake: Do not collect highly soluble gases over water.

questions.prompt: The suitable drying agent for ammonia is:
questions.answer: quicklime
questions.explanation: Quicklime (CaO) is basic and dries ammonia without reacting with it.
questions.commonMistake: Acidic drying agents react with basic ammonia.

questions.prompt: Ammonia reacts with hydrogen chloride to form:
questions.answer: ammonium chloride fumes
questions.explanation: NH3 and HCl combine directly to produce dense white fumes of NH4Cl.
questions.commonMistake: This is a standard test for both ammonia and HCl.

questions.prompt: When excess NH4OH is added to CuSO4 solution, the observation is:
options: pale blue precipitate dissolving to deep blue solution
questions.answer: pale blue precipitate dissolving to deep blue solution
questions.explanation: Copper(II) hydroxide dissolves in excess ammonia forming a deep blue complex.
questions.commonMistake: Note the change from precipitate to deep blue solution in excess.

questions.prompt: Ammonia is prepared in the laboratory by heating ammonium chloride with:
questions.answer: calcium hydroxide
questions.explanation: An alkali reacts with an ammonium salt on heating to liberate ammonia gas.
questions.commonMistake: Acids do not liberate ammonia from ammonium salts.

questions.prompt: Moist red litmus paper in ammonia turns:
questions.answer: blue
questions.explanation: Ammonia forms an alkaline solution in moisture, turning red litmus blue.
questions.commonMistake: Moisture is needed for the litmus change.

questions.prompt: In the reaction 2NH3 + 3CuO → 3Cu + 3H2O + N2, ammonia acts as:
questions.answer: a reducing agent
questions.explanation: Ammonia reduces copper(II) oxide to copper and is itself oxidised to nitrogen.
questions.commonMistake: Identify which substance loses oxygen or is oxidised.

questions.prompt: Why is concentrated sulphuric acid not used to dry ammonia gas?
options: It converts ammonia to nitrogen only
questions.answer: It reacts with ammonia
questions.explanation: Concentrated sulphuric acid is acidic and reacts with basic ammonia instead of merely drying it.
questions.commonMistake: Drying agents must be chemically compatible with the gas.

questions.prompt: Aqueous solution of ammonia is commonly called ammonium ________.
questions.answer: hydroxide
questions.explanation: Ammonia dissolves in water to form an alkaline solution represented as NH4OH.
questions.commonMistake: Ammonium hydroxide in solution is weakly alkaline.

questions.prompt: The gas collected by upward delivery must be ________ than air.
questions.answer: lighter
questions.explanation: Lighter gases rise and displace air downwards in upward delivery.
questions.commonMistake: Denser gases are collected by downward delivery.

questions.prompt: Dense white fumes of ________ are formed when ammonia meets hydrogen chloride.
questions.answer: ammonium chloride
questions.explanation: NH3 and HCl combine to form solid NH4Cl seen as white fumes.
questions.commonMistake: Use the correct name of the ammonium salt formed.

questions.prompt: Write the balanced equation for laboratory preparation of ammonia from ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide.
questions.answer: 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 → CaCl2 + 2H2O + 2NH3↑
questions.explanation: Heating an ammonium salt with an alkali liberates ammonia gas.
questions.commonMistake: Balance all atoms including nitrogen, hydrogen and chlorine.

questions.prompt: Why is ammonia not collected over water?
questions.answer: Ammonia is highly soluble in water, so it would dissolve instead of being collected. Therefore it is collected by upward delivery (downward displacement of air).
questions.explanation: Collection method must prevent loss of gas by dissolution.
questions.commonMistake: Mention high solubility as the key reason.

questions.prompt: Describe the fountain experiment with ammonia and state what it proves.
questions.answer: A flask filled with dry ammonia is fitted with a jet dipping into red litmus solution. When a small amount of water enters the flask, ammonia dissolves rapidly, lowering pressure and causing the solution to rush in as a fountain. The solution turns blue, proving that ammonia is highly soluble in water and forms an alkaline solution.
questions.explanation: Both solubility and basic nature are demonstrated in one experiment.
questions.commonMistake: State the colour change of litmus clearly.

questions.prompt: State the observations when ammonia solution is added dropwise and then in excess to copper(II) sulphate solution.
questions.answer: On dropwise addition, a pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide is formed. On adding excess ammonia solution, the precipitate dissolves to give a deep blue solution.
questions.explanation: Complex ion formation in excess ammonia causes the precipitate to dissolve.
questions.commonMistake: Report both stages: dropwise and excess.

questions.prompt: Describe the laboratory preparation, drying and collection of ammonia gas with reasons for each step.
questions.answer: Heat a mixture of ammonium chloride and calcium hydroxide in a flask to produce ammonia: 2NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 → CaCl2 + 2H2O + 2NH3↑. Pass the gas through quicklime to dry it, as quicklime absorbs moisture without reacting with basic ammonia. Collect the gas by upward delivery because ammonia is lighter than air and highly soluble in water, so it cannot be collected over water.
questions.explanation: Choice of drying agent and collection method depends on ammonia’s properties.
questions.commonMistake: Do not use concentrated sulphuric acid or collect over water.

questions.prompt: Explain the reducing action of ammonia on heated copper(II) oxide with equation and observations.
questions.answer: When dry ammonia is passed over heated black copper(II) oxide, ammonia reduces it to reddish-brown copper while ammonia is oxidised to nitrogen and water: 2NH3 + 3CuO → 3Cu + 3H2O + N2. The black solid turns reddish-brown and water droplets may be seen in cooler parts of the apparatus. This shows ammonia acting as a reducing agent.
questions.explanation: Colour change from black CuO to reddish-brown Cu indicates reduction.
questions.commonMistake: Balance the equation and identify both products from ammonia.

questions.prompt: Compare the action of ammonium hydroxide solution on solutions of (i) copper(II) sulphate, (ii) zinc sulphate and (iii) iron(III) chloride.
questions.answer: (i) With copper(II) sulphate, NH4OH gives a pale blue precipitate of Cu(OH)2 that dissolves in excess to form a deep blue solution. (ii) With zinc sulphate, it gives a white gelatinous precipitate of Zn(OH)2 that dissolves in excess to form a colourless solution. (iii) With iron(III) chloride, it gives a reddish-brown precipitate of Fe(OH)3 that is insoluble in excess. These differences help identify the metal ions.
questions.explanation: Excess reagent behaviour distinguishes Cu2+ and Zn2+ from Fe3+.
questions.commonMistake: State initial precipitate and behaviour in excess for each ion.

questions.prompt: A gas turns moist red litmus blue and forms dense white fumes with HCl. Identify the gas and give the equation for the fume formation.
questions.answer: The gas is ammonia. It is alkaline in moist conditions, turning red litmus blue, and reacts with hydrogen chloride to form dense white fumes of ammonium chloride: NH3 + HCl → NH4Cl.
questions.explanation: Both tests together confirm the identity of ammonia.
questions.commonMistake: Use moist litmus because dry ammonia may not change dry litmus readily.

questions.prompt: A student dries ammonia gas by passing it through concentrated sulphuric acid and collects it over water. Identify and correct the errors.
questions.answer: Concentrated sulphuric acid is acidic and reacts with basic ammonia, so it cannot be used as a drying agent; quicklime should be used instead. Ammonia is highly soluble in water, so it cannot be collected over water; it should be collected by upward delivery. Correcting these steps ensures ammonia is obtained dry and without loss.
questions.explanation: Preparation methods must match the chemical and physical properties of the gas.
questions.commonMistake: Check compatibility of drying agent with the gas being prepared.

questions.prompt: How would you distinguish between aqueous ammonia and sodium hydroxide solution using a copper(II) salt solution?
questions.answer: Add each alkali dropwise and then in excess to copper(II) sulphate solution. With sodium hydroxide, a pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide forms and remains insoluble in excess NaOH. With aqueous ammonia, a pale blue precipitate forms initially but dissolves in excess ammonia to give a deep blue solution. The deep blue solution in excess distinguishes aqueous ammonia from sodium hydroxide.
questions.explanation: Complex formation with ammonia causes dissolution not seen with NaOH.
questions.commonMistake: Compare behaviour in excess reagent, not just the initial precipitate.

questions.prompt: Explain why ammonia solution can precipitate metal hydroxides from salt solutions.
questions.answer: Ammonia dissolves in water to form ammonium hydroxide, which provides hydroxide ions in solution: NH3 + H2O ⇌ NH4+ + OH−. These OH− ions react with metal ions such as Fe3+, Cu2+ or Zn2+ to form insoluble metal hydroxides that appear as precipitates. The extent and solubility in excess depend on the metal ion involved.
questions.explanation: Hydroxide ions from aqueous ammonia are responsible for precipitation reactions.
questions.commonMistake: Relate precipitation to availability of OH− ions, not ammonia molecules alone.
